HEADLINE: How the new wage subsidy works
TEXT:
Tens of thousands of workers already stood down or retrenched will be eligible for the Morrison government's $130 billion wage subsidy scheme, with employers to begin being reimbursed from May.

Even employers whose business has been shut down on government orders will receive money to pay employees who cannot do any meaningful work or attend their workplace.

Under the JobKeeper payment scheme, employees will have their wage subsidised by $1500 a fortnight, irrespective of their normal paypacket. It is different to the UK's approach, which is subsidising wages by a fixed 80 per cent of a person's wage.

Australia's scheme covers employees who are full or part-time, or a casual with at least 12 months of service as of March 1 this year. It also captures sole traders.

Businesses with a turnover under $1 billion that have seen their revenue tumble by at least 30 per cent will be eligible to access the scheme.

Larger companies with a turnover of more than $1 billion will need to have sustained a 50 per cent reduction to tap into funds.

The $1500 payment is equivalent to 70 per cent of the median wage, or roughly 100 per cent of the median in the hospitality, tourism and retail sectors, which have borne the brunt of the job losses.

"This payment will give working Australians their best chance of keeping their job and keeping them connected to their employers so that they can bounce back in the recovery phase," Treasurer Josh Frydenberg said.

For a business still operating, they must continue to pay their staff their regular income but will receive the $1500 payment to subsidise each wage. They will continue to have to pay the superannuation guarantee on their employees' income.

For a business that has stood down employees, the employer will be required to pay them a minimum $1500 a fortnight. Paying the superannuation guarantee is at the employer's discretion in this case.

An employee kept on a company's books in this case may not have any work for them to do - for example a chef in a restaurant - but would be encouraged to stay engaged with the business.

In an indication of how generous the scheme can be, workers already earning less than $1500 a fortnight, stand to receive a pay rise. A part-time worker being paid $1000 a fortnight would still attract the full $1500 subsidy, with an employer not allowed to pocket the difference.

The scheme also applies to workers who have been retrenched rather than stood down. If they are rehired their employer will receive the $1500 subsidy.

While the scheme needs legislation, the subsidy started immediately on March 30. The Australian Tax Office will pay the subsidy monthly in arrears to employers, with the first payments to be made in the first week of May.

An employer will be responsible for applying to the ATO to receive subsidies, and will need to show they have suffered a downturn. They will also be required monthly to report how many employees are being supported.

HEADLINE: Collapse averted for now, says sector
TEXT:
A childcare sector that was on the verge of mass stand-downs says the Prime Minister's jobkeeper package will help businesses keep their staff even as attendance falls close to zero.

The industry employs more than 180,000 staff but attendance has collapsed, with some centres reporting 90 per cent of families have withdrawn children from care. One provider reported only one child out of 60 enrolments had arrived for care yesterday.

"This is a step in the right direction. There are still gaps which we are going to fill but it means we can keep employees in productive work," said the chief executive of the Early Learning and Care Council of Australia, Elizabeth Death.

"The incredibly important thing is we get to keep qualified staff. We've been worried once we stood people down we would never be able to find qualified people to re-employ once conditions turned around."

Ms Death said the money meant a "significant number of employees" would be retained by childcare providers and some families that were cutting back on childcare for fear of losing income would be prepared to put their children back into care.

"Let's call it the first step towards survival for the sector," she said. "We're looking forward to working with the government to keep the early childhood sector afloat.

"Don't forget there are lots of other costs we are going to have to find. Rent is a big one for most of our members."

Ms Death said very few of her members would have a problem meeting the government's criteria of a fall in turnover of more than 30 per cent since the beginning of March, and none breached the cut-off point of $1 billion in turnover.

HEADLINE: The $214b question: how are we going to pay for this?
TEXT:
It was only 20 days ago that Scott Morrison appealed to corporate Australia to do its utmost to hold on to its workers throughout the coronavirus crisis.

Addressing The Australian Financial Review Business Summit, Morrison signalled that while government's then-impending $17.6 billion stimulus package, to be released a few days later, would look after small and medium business and their workers, the corporates should draw on their vast reserves to look after their own.

"Hold onto your people, you will need them on the other side. Wherever possible, support them - whether full-time, part-time, or casual - including with paid leave if they need to take time off due to the virus," he said.

In the three weeks since, the virus-induced economic ruin has been so rapacious that the corporates have had to stand down tens of thousands of workers and the government is picking up the wage bill. Big Time.

The $130 billion outlay announced yesterday in the form of $1500 fortnightly payments for as many as 6 million people over the next six months, takes to $214 billion now rolled out in three packages in less than 20 days.

Perhaps Morrison was mindful of the first thought many had when he dropped the big number just after 4pm yesterday. How are we going to pay for this?

Without prompting, the PM reassured that the economy would survive this, but the same could not be said for others.

"Our goal is to protect the lives and livelihoods of Australians, to protect and preserve the very economy that we will depend on so significantly in the months ahead, and on the other side as well, for the generations that will follow us out of this," he said.

"Many countries, in the months ahead and perhaps beyond that, may well see their economies collapse. Some may see them hollow out. In the very worst or circumstances, we could see countries themselves fall into chaos.

"This will not be Australia."

Tellingly, after three packages worth a combined $214 billion, Morrison expressed hope that this would be the last major bailout needed.

But there were no guarantees.

"We must work together to make this work and to make it go as far as possible," he said.

"We still do not know the many other challenges we will face in the months ahead. And our decisions have been calibrated to that end."

One danger of all this spending is that we have quickly become inured to the scale of the numbers involved.

HEADLINE: 'We're bloody lucky we've got them': from pariahs to saviours
TEXT:
The pledge made by the big banks to back their customers is about to be tested when they start choosing which businesses to save or let fail, as the biggest demand shock in nearly 100 years batters the economy.

Bank chief executives including Commonwealth Bank's Matt Comyn, NAB's Ross McEwan and ANZ's Shayne Elliott said the scale of the task ahead of them was becoming clear as they sorted through 170,000 requests from households and businesses affected by the COVID-19 outbreak to defer loan repayments.

Speaking at The Australian Financial Review Banking & Wealth Summit crisis briefing, which was conducted online from locations around the country, the bank chiefs said they would do their best to save as many customers and businesses as possible.

Reserve Bank of Australia board member Ian Harper said this was critical to restore confidence in the financial system.

"This is a moment when the banks, in a way, can redeem themselves," Professor Harper said.

Just 12 months after warning the banks were at risk as the backlash from the Hayne royal commission reached a crescendo, Fidelity Australia portfolio manager Kate Howitt said banks were leading the way on COVID-19.

"Of course a year on, here we are, and it turns out they are the cookie jar of the nation - and we're bloody lucky we've got them," Ms Howitt said.

She said the banking royal commission would be seen as a catalyst for change, forcing the banks to adopt a community-first mindset just in time for the crisis.

"We're going to look back and say, 'Well thank God they did that'," Ms Howitt said.

Mr Comyn said the bank had been forced over the past week to double its estimate on the hit to GDP based on real-time payment data for the March quarter, with another and potentially much steeper contraction to come.

"There is no question there will be a substantial demand shock," he said. "That is why the base case for the March quarter is something like a 10 per cent contraction in the economy."

Mr Comyn cited forecasts in the US for a 25 per cent contraction in the June quarter but said the depth and breadth of any recession would depend on how long containment measures were in place.

The impact of the fallout from an inevitable spike in bad debts on bank capital was "impossible to forecast" and Mr Comyn said the capital regime was a credit to the prudential regulator APRA and its chairman Wayne Byres.

"Having very well-capitalised banks with lots of liquidity is fantastic at this point in the cycle," Mr Comyn said. "The reality is we're going to need it."

But the bank chiefs said capital was not unlimited, and banks would need to be selective on the businesses they chose to save or let fail.

Mr Elliott said banks had large balance sheets but their resources were finite. ANZ had no interest in supporting already failing businesses, creating a "zombie economy", because doing so would be "failing the community".

"One of the responsibilities we have is we have become the ICU unit of the economy," he said. "These corporates and households will come into intensive care, and we will have this unfortunate role at some point of having to decide who comes out at the other end.

"The reality is even though we are incredibly resourceful and we have large balance sheets and capability, we can't do everything and so we're going to have to apply our resources, our balance sheet, to help those that really do have sustainable business models."

Mr McEwan, fresh from launching NAB's SME coronavirus loans of up to $250,000 at rates of 4.5 per cent, said the bank would concentrate on looking after the customers it knew had robust pre-crisis businesses.

"Certainly for us, we're going to be looking to support our existing customers," he said.

Mr McEwan said the bank would selectively lend to businesses with acquisition strategies but first needed to support loyal customers.

He expected NAB's net profit to be "knocked around". It might not show up in the current quarter but as the shocks grew "you'll see it certainly in our next half".

The pledge to support strong businesses landed just a few hours before it was revealed ANZ and NAB had formed a syndicate to lend the Australian Football League - which suspended the season just a week earlier - more than half a billion dollars.

Competition chief Rod Sims said the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission was taking extraordinary steps including allowing banks to work together on how to support businesses and was optimistic about a rebound.

"I think once the recovery is over there'll be this spring back in demand which I suspect might well surprise us on the upside," he said. "Once the crisis is over measures can be unwound and that's the best way to get recovery - losing competitive dynamic through this crisis would be a tragedy."

The ACCC mergers team would not be facilitating any opportunistic mergers, with Mr Sims saying any deterioration in the competitive market structure would be a "tragedy".

"There's no chance of us taking a lenient approach," he said.

Mr Comyn said Australia was fortunate that government finances were in "excellent shape" and "I personally don't believe there's any imminent risk of a downgrade [by ratings agencies ] at the sovereign level. I think again, fortunately, where we start from is a very strong position."

He also said all measures introduced to support the economy needed to be matched with a capability to implement them: "You can design a very attractive scheme, but if you can't practically implement it and get money flowing to employees and businesses, then it's just a concept on paper."

AMP CEO Francesco De Ferrari was more cautious, drawing on the experience of family members in Italy who described the fight against the virus as "like war". He said Australia's island status was an advantage and likely to slow the spread of infection.

APRA capability review author and former ACCC chairman Graeme Samuel said Australian banks were in a position to prove confidence in them was not misplaced.

Reserve Bank board member Ian Harper agreed, saying the conditions were right for the banks to prove they had learned their lessons and deliver a "redemption moment. If they do that, then I reckon a lot of sins will be forgiven."

HEADLINE: $130b to save six million jobs
TEXT:
Almost half the Australian workforce will receive $1500 a fortnight for the next six months under a record $130 billion wage subsidy, news of which drove the biggest jump in the sharemarket for 40 years.

Unveiling the massive bailout, Prime Minister Scott Morrison expressed hope, but could not guarantee, it would will be the last major spending package needed to deal with the coronavirus crisis.

Described by the Prime Minister as an "economic lifeline", the subsidy, known as the JobKeeper Payment, takes to $214 billion now allocated towards stimulus and support measures in three separate packages in less than three weeks. This amounts to about 11 per cent of GDP.

More expense will be incurred later this week when the government announces a series of rent-relief measures which will involve, in some cases, state and federal governments giving tax relief to landlords in return for waiving or cutting rents.

Within an hour of the announcement, the government reported 8000 businesses had registered for the JobKeeper Payment.

Business groups lauded the payment, which is 70 per cent of the median wage, as a job saver, while the ACTU and the Greens derided it as insufficient.

The local sharemarket surged 2.4 per cent in the last 10 minutes of trading as news of the $130 billion payment was released. The S&P/ASX 200 Index finished up 339 points or 7 per cent to 5181.4. The late jump added $35 billion to the value of the sharemarket, which posted a massive $102 billion gain for the day.

The government and Labor are discussing reconvening Parliament as early as next week to rush through the necessary legislation for the payment, which is the centrepiece of the "hibernation" strategy, which involves allowing businesses to start up once the crisis ends while accruing no liabilities in the interim.

Mr Morrison and Treasurer Josh Frydenberg announced that an estimated six million people - those sacked or stood down since March 1, as well as those still working for struggling small, medium and big businesses - would be eligible for the payment, which is designed to keep workers and businesses connected.

The money is a flat payment, meaning everybody receives the same amount, regardless of current or previous income, and it will be paid to employers through the Australian Tax Office.

To be eligible, companies with turnovers of less than $1 billion must have lost at least 30 per cent of turnover, while those with turnovers of more than $1 billion, such as airlines, must be down by at least 50 per cent.

The employer must then use the payment to subsidise wages for those still working, or pay it directly to those who are stood down but are still on the books.

If a worker has been retrenched since March 1, the employer can put them back on the books so they become eligible for the payment.

This would disqualify them from the separate welfare wage of a maximum of $1100 a fortnight, known as the JobSeeker payment, which is administered through Centrelink.

For people who will still be dependent on the welfare wage, the government also on Monday lifted from $48,000 to $79,762 the amount an unemployed person's partner can earn before they become ineligible for the benefit.

The new $1500 JobKeeper Payment is effective immediately. It will be taxed like normal income but there will be no superannuation guarantee payable on the money.

Those eligible are full-time and part-time workers as well as casuals who have been with the same employer for 12 months. Sole traders and the not-for-profit sector are included.

The payment will be made to eligible businesses in the first week of May as monthly arrears from the Tax Office. The businesses can either start paying workers now, if they have the cash flow, or backpay them to March 30 when the money arrives.

Small and medium businesses, defined by having turnovers of less than $50 million, will still be eligible for the previously announced cash payments of up to $100,000, which is also administered through the ATO.

Unveiling the package, Mr Morrison expressed hope that businesses can begin distributing the JobKeeper Payment immediately and will be reimbursed from the first week of May.

Expressing hope no government ever again will have to blow the budget in such fashion, Mr Morrison said "we are living in unprecedented times".

"We fight against a virus and against the economic ruin that it can threaten," he said. "This calls for unprecedented action - governments making decisions like they never have before."

Mr Morrison sought to reassure that the massive outlay was affordable, even if it will take years to repay.

"Our goal is to protect the lives and livelihoods of Australians, to protect and preserve the very economy that we will depend on so significantly in the months ahead, and on the other side as well, for the generations that will follow us out of this," he said.

"Many countries, in the months ahead and perhaps beyond that, may well see their economies collapse. Some may see them hollow out. In the very worst or circumstances, we could see countries themselves fall into chaos. This will not be Australia."

Mr Morrison expressed hope no more giant packages would be needed.

"We must work together to make this work and to make it go as far as possible," he said.

"We still do not know the many other challenges we will face in the months ahead. And our decisions have been calibrated to that end."

Commonwealth Bank of Australia chief executive Matt Comyn called the package "extraordinary".

"It means the safety net for those most in need is now wider, deeper and stronger. It will help many more businesses stay afloat, many more people keep their jobs and enable us all to rebound stronger and sooner when the crisis has passed," he said.

Still to come later this week will be a package of measures to save people and businesses being evicted if they are unable to pay their rents.

The states have already announced they will legislate a moratorium on forced evictions for six months.

To help commercial and residential landlords, the banks have agreed to mortgage relief measures while the states are offering to lift land taxes for various periods and the Commonwealth is looking at what tax levers it can pull.

On Monday, the banks extended the six-month deferral of loan repayments for small business, homeowners and investment property landlords to another 30,000 businesses, taking the overall value of loans for coronavirus support to $250 billion.

HEADLINE: Flexibility deal to help rescue restaurant jobs
TEXT:
Restaurants and cafes will be able to reduce workers' minimum hours and have greater powers to force staff to take leave as part of a new deal to save jobs during the coronavirus crisis.

Restaurant & Catering Australia and the United Workers Union reached a deal yesterday to suspend workplace conditions in the restaurant award as businesses lay off thousands of staff while shutting down or shifting to a delivery and takeaway model.

The agreement comes as it was revealed that the retail industry is seeking its own award flexibility, and follows similar changes last week for more than a million hotel and administrative workers.

The restaurant award covers more than 450,000 workers at some 43,000 restaurants and cafes across the country, with the employer group estimating two-thirds of those businesses have stayed open during the crisis.

The industry association's chief executive Wes Lambert said "these changes will no doubt keep businesses open and keep Australians in jobs".

"The changes agreed to in the restaurant award build on the changes in the hospitality award but go further to ensure greater flexibility for businesses that cannot make the transition to takeaway and delivery during the COVID-19 crisis," he said.

The deal largely mirrors the one reached by the hotel industry last week, including relaxing classifications and annual leave restrictions, and reducing full-time minimum hours to 22.8 hours a week and part-time hours to 60 per cent of guaranteed hours.

Employers will also be able to direct staff to take leave in the case of a business shutdown with one week's notice, down from the original four weeks.

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry workplace director Scott Barklamb said the temporary changes would allow restaurants and cafes to "scale up or down their operations and employees to work fluidly across other areas of the business, providing they have the training to do so".

"Greater flexibility means these businesses might just be able to survive this harsh trading environment," he said.

The changes have been filed before the Fair Work Commission for urgent approval.

Meanwhile, retail industry bodies have approached the Shop Distributive and Allied Employees Association to suspend conditions in the retail award.

SDA national secretary Gerard Dwyer said the union would "engage in discussions to deal with the special circumstances".

He added: "Circumstances vary widely across the retail sector . . . supermarket chains have been very busy; the opposite is the case for much of the discretionary retail sector. Arrangements need to be tailored accordingly."

HEADLINE: Morrison's $130b bet to save economy
TEXT:
NAB chief executive Ross McEwan acknowledges the startling new reality dominating every waking hour - and the many sleepless nights - of governments, bankers and all other business owners.

"There is no playbook for this," McEwan says.

Instead, the constant risk has been that the play is moving far too quickly for the latest rules of engagement to be sufficiently effective to cushion escalating carnage.

This column does not underestimate the pressure or the demands on governments and businesses trying to operate at speed to deliver actions deemed unfathomable just a month ago.

But too often, the notion of "whatever it takes" in terms of new government assistance has already had to be translated into "too little too late" within a week or so. Doing more with more - rather than with less - goes counter to traditional Treasury thinking, of course. Still, the risk of underspending in the face of such an avalanche of destruction seems greater than that of excessive expenditure.

So the government's announcement yesterday was for a huge $130 billion economic package in order to subsidise wages over six months. This is a truly massive spend and should help shore up the economy as well as restore a degree of consumer and business confidence about the immediate financial future.

Scott Morrison has gone from calling the newest government measure a "bridge" to the other side to an "economic lifeline" for up to 6 million Australians to make it through the coronavirus crisis.

It will provide employees $1500 a fortnight, paid via their employers through the ATO, in a new "jobkeeper" payment. That adds up to $39,000 a year, backdated to March 30 and payable from May, for full-time and part-time employees and sole traders as well as casuals with the same employer for at least a year. It will also apply to those people stood down from March 1. The threshold for businesses is to have lost 30 per cent of their revenue over a month or 50 per cent for those with previous revenue of over $1 billion.

The government says this version of wages subsidy is more generous than that offered by New Zealand and broader than the arrangements on offer in Britain.

Yet it is already under fire, including friendly fire from some business leaders, for being too low to help the problem it seeks to address - that is, giving businesses enough space to hold onto most of their staff despite the collapse of revenue and cash flow, while providing individuals sufficient shelter from the trauma of unemployment or financial ruin.

"Some will say it is too little, some will say it is too much," Morrison acknowledged.

Will it be enough? The Prime Minister insists it is a uniquely Australian solution and based on enduring national values and principles. In particular, that includes the flat rate of payment rather than a percentage to avoid previously higher-paid people getting more assistance.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg also points out that for many people in the sectors hardest hit in retail, hospitality and tourism, the payment will add up to close to 100 per cent of their previous minimum wages.

Canberra's desperate hope is that people will stay connected to their previous employers even if the businesses do close. But the government aim is for the payment to also allow many more businesses to stay open and keep employees working - to some extent at least.

Getting an impossible balance as right as possible doesn't just require extraordinarily difficult judgments by governments about what is required. The approach of the banks will also be crucial.

And while Australia's big banks are deeply empathetic to the plight of their business customers, big and small, they are still sending a tough message to some. The banks won't be able to save everyone. It is going to be about assessing and assisting those with the best chance of surviving the sudden onset of immediate and massive financial haemorrhaging.

ANZ chief executive Shayne Elliott told The Australian Financial Review Banking & Wealth Summit crisis briefing yesterday that about 10 per cent of the bank's 130,000 small business customers have sought the six-month deferral of interest and principle payments now available. Ross McEwan estimates the figure to be about 8 per cent of NAB's business customers. But that is only so far.

The bankers know the extraordinary speed and size of that change over the past week will only accelerate over the next few weeks. Using the now familiar language of the health crisis, Elliott says the aim is to try to "isolate" the spread of infection as much as possible by limiting the amount of problems in one area flowing through to another.

Community and political scepticism about the big banks for being too big, too dominant, too profitable has been abruptly replaced by relief their balance sheets and mindsets are in relatively good shape to provide vital life support for stricken businesses and households.

According to McEwan, NAB will prioritise existing customers and continue to support good businesses while still protecting the bank's balance sheet. But he also makes the point that his experience in Britain has shown it is better to be honest with customers that were already struggling "sooner rather than later".

Banking leaders generally support the government's moves to steadily ramp up assistance, including the abrupt about-turn on the need for wage subsidies to partially insulate businesses and individual incomes being lost.

According to the CBA's Matt Comyn, providing an incentive for businesses to pay employees is essential given the importance of maintaining connection.

"So that when we come out of these containment measures, hopefully large parts of the economy can be stood up relatively quickly," he told the Summit.

Hopefully.

HEADLINE: $130b could save up to 80pc of GDP collapse
TEXT:
Australia's largest single fiscal stimulus package in history could save between 66 and 80 per cent of the forecast collapse in gross domestic product, economists say in very early estimates.

"When the house is on fire you save the furniture," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Michael Blythe said. "And I would say this goes a fair way in filling the hole that some have expected would be left in GDP from the virus."

The $130 billion in wage subsidies announced by the Morrison government equates to 6.65 per cent of GDP. Total fiscal stimulus so far is $214 billion, or more than 11 per cent of GDP.

Combined with the $105 billion from the Reserve Bank and other fiscal measures the total stimulus tally is now $320 billion, or 16.4 per cent of GDP.

Economists had forecast an unemployment rate as high as 16 per cent and a hit to GDP in the June quarter alone of 9.7 per cent.

Australia's recreation, hospitality and tourism sectors are worth a combined 14 per cent of GDP. Assuming those sectors take the full economic hit, then the JobKeeper Payment - the latest wage subsidy rescue package of $130 billion - would save two-thirds of that 14 per cent GDP damage, according to HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham.

"If you focus purely on fiscal stimulus that is not loan-related, then the government has now announced total stimulus of 9.8 per cent of GDP.

"So this goes some way to fulfilling that 14 per cent hit to GDP," Mr Bloxham said.

AMP Capital's Shane Oliver said the package could go as far as preventing 80 per cent of the fall off in GDP.

"We are expecting a 12 per cent contraction in GDP spread across the March and June quarters due to coronavirus - mainly due to the shutdowns."

He said the total fiscal stimulus however now amounted to more than 10 per cent of GDP.

"So while the fiscal stimulus won't stop the contraction in the short term - because people are stuck at home not spending - it will provide an offset for over 80 per cent of the hit to GDP and holds out the promise of a decent rebound for when we can get out and spend again."

In Australia, a rule of thumb is that for every 125,000 job losses, the unemployment rate rises by around 1 percentage point. Unemployment was 5.1 per cent in February.

"Prior to today's announcement, unemployment was expected to hit double digits in coming months.The peak is now likely to be somewhat lower, although under-employment and few hours worked will remain an issue," EY chief economist Jo Masters said.

"It will help the economy but it's important to remember it will cushion - not fully offset - the expected hit to consumption from weakness in the labour market."

The $1500-a-fortnight wage subsidy being offered by the federal government will go to as many as 6 million workers.

It will provide the equivalent of around 70 per cent of the national median wage. For workers in the accommodation, hospitality and retail sectors it will equate to full replacement for a median wage.

HEADLINE: Big four funds freeze premiums
TEXT:
Australia's four biggest health insurers, Medibank, Bupa, HCF and NIB, have scrapped plans to increase premiums on April 1, in recognition of the financial hardship facing many members as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The insurers were following the lead of West Australian not-for-profit fund HBF, which announced it would freeze premiums last week. As a result most Australians with private health cover will see no rise for at least six months.

The flurry of announcements follows last week's government ban on all non-urgent elective surgeries.

The decision, intended to free up the health system to deal with the coronavirus crisis, will almost certainly result in a significant drop in private health insurance claims.

Medibank cited the ban when it announced its decision on Sunday night.

JAMES FERNYHOUGH
